title: Trump Administration’s English-Only Head Start Edict Is Bad for Young Learners d-for-young-learners/
author: Shantel Meek and Conor P. Williams
summary: Shantel Meek and Conor P. Williams argue that the Trump administration's proposed English-only mandate for Head Start classrooms contradicts evidence, law, and the administration's own goals. They describe Head Start's 61-year record of serving about 40 million children, with dual language learners among its greatest beneficiaries, and note that a 1975 requirement for bilingual staff was sustained by administrations of both parties. The authors explain that bilingual early learning is the educational gold standard for children who speak another language at home, because developing a first language makes children stronger language learners and speeds English acquisition. They add that the mandate would cost $73 million to $124 million in restaffing and materials, and question why tribal communities are exempted but not other language groups. Finally, they warn that trading quality for more seats would hollow out what makes Head Start effective.
points: About a third of Head Start's roughly 800,000 enrollees are dual language learners.
Bilingual staffing requirements date to the Ford administration and survived the first Trump administration.
Research shows developing children's first language helps them acquire English more fully and rapidly.
Texas's long investment in bilingual education helps its English learners outperform peers in most states on NAEP.
The administration's own estimate puts implementation costs at $73 million to $124 million.
quotes: That’s why the Trump administration’s recent proposal to enact a national English-only mandate in Head Start classrooms is so mistaken.
Today, about a third of Head Start’s roughly 800,000 enrollees are dual language learners.
Studies are unambiguous: for the nearly one-third of Head Start attendees that speak a non-English language at home, bilingual learning is the educational gold standard.

That is, by developing their first languages more deeply, they become more confident language users, more able to understand complex elements of grammar, syntax, and the like. Over time, these stronger language competencies help them to more thoroughly and rapidly acquire English.
On the Nation’s Report Card, ELs in Texas routinely score better in math and English language arts than their peers in almost every other state.

And at some point, once safety, quality, and the high standard of care that has made Head Start the national guidepost are dissolved — we need to ask ourselves what exactly are we expanding access to?
